newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Traders in dark over new Thai reference rate.
newsitem.headline: Traders in dark over new Thai reference rate.

text.p: Foreign exchange traders contacted in Singapore by Reuters said they had no idea where the Bank of Thailand would be setting its new baht reference rate against the U.S. dollar.
"I have absolutely no idea. It could be anywhere. A managed float means loads of things," the head of trading at a European house in Singapore said.

Earlier on Wednesday financial markets in Asia were stunned by news the Bank of Thailand had decided to let "the value of the baht...be determined by market forces to reflect fundamental economic forces."
The traders said this amounted to a de facto devaluation although prior to today the Bank of Thailand had strenuously denied the currency would be devalued.

The foreign exchange announcement was accompanied by a two percentage point increase in Thailand's discount rate -- the rate at which the central bank lends to commercial banks -- from 10.5 percent to 12.5 percent.
The central bank said it would henceforth publish a baht/dollar reference rate based on the baht's trading average the day before.
It said it had an "appropriate rate" in mind in which it expected the baht to move. However, it did not say when it would publish the first reference rate.

"We've seen the various statements (from the Bank of Thailand) during the day, but when is the first (reference) rate coming onto the screens? Where the baht trades is dependent on this," a dealer at another European bank in Singapore commented.

The problem is that some traders believe the Thai authorities will opt for an immediate devalution and set the new rate accordingly lower while others believe they will opt for a more gradual approach.
It's extremely hard to say what they are going to do," said one Singapore based analyst. "With the old system you could make certain assumptions, with this new system you cannot."
Under the old system the baht was fixed against a basket of currencies -- which the Bank of Thailand never revealed -- and kept within a four satang range around it.

But the dealer at the European bank said, "The whole ballgame has changed. Sure the spot market's been whippy but there's not much trade been done. Everyone's waiting for the (central) bank to tell us what's happening."
The confusion over both the timing, and the actual level, of the reference rate typified the baht market of the last five or six weeks, traders said.

"The head of trading at the European firm commented, "We, like so many people, have been on the sidelines since it (the baht) all went wobbly back in May. I'm going to wait and see the reference rate before I do anything."
